intro.title:
Chat system
WhatsApp / Slack-style
intro.subtitle: Persistent sockets, a durable log and workers: one checkmark when Kafka has the message, two when Boris's phone does.

cues.cap: Designing a chat system in the style of WhatsApp, Slack or Messenger, message by message.
Three layers: a stateful layer that only holds the sockets, a durable log for the messages, and workers that do everything else. Let's send 'Hello' from Anna to Boris.

scenes.title: Stateful sockets, a durable log, stateless workers

steps.cap: The send path: Anna's phone talks over an already open WebSocket, through an L4 load balancer, to a WebSocket Gateway server, which calls Chat Service over gRPC; Chat Service checks Redis and writes to Kafka.
steps.say: The send path: Anna's phone talks over an already open websocket, through a layer four load balancer, to a WebSocket Gateway server, which calls Chat Service over G R P C; Chat Service checks Redis and writes to Kafka.
steps.title: Send path
steps.note: Only the WebSocket Gateway holds state, and only open sockets: about 450 instances with up to 50k connections each.

steps.cap: Everything after Kafka is asynchronous and runs as independent consumer groups: Delivery Worker finds Boris's sessions and forwards, Persist Worker writes the history to Cassandra, Push Worker notifies offline devices through FCM or APNs.
steps.say: Everything after Kafka is asynchronous and runs as independent consumer groups: Delivery Worker finds Boris's sessions and forwards, Persist Worker writes the history to Cassandra, Push Worker notifies offline devices through F C M or A P N s.
steps.title: Consumer groups
steps.note: Three readers of the same log: a slow Cassandra never delays delivery, and a flood of pushes never delays persistence.

steps.cap: History and resynchronisation go over plain HTTPS REST: API Gateway, Chat Service, Cassandra. The socket is for live traffic; the log and the history are the truth.
steps.say: History and resynchronisation go over plain H T T P S rest: A P I Gateway, Chat Service, Cassandra. The socket is for live traffic; the log and the history are the truth.
steps.title: REST path
steps.note: since=<seq> is the whole resync protocol: a monotonic number per chat makes gaps and duplicates detectable on the client.

scenes.title: From Anna's Enter to Boris's two checkmarks

steps.cap: Anna types 'Hello' and presses Enter. Her phone already has a WebSocket open to WS-Server-12, so the message travels over it, without a new TCP or TLS handshake, carrying a client_msg_id generated on the phone before the first attempt.
steps.say: Anna types Hello and presses Enter. Her phone already has a websocket open to W S Server twelve, so the message travels over it, without a new T C P or T L S handshake, carrying a client message I D generated on the phone before the first attempt.
steps.title: Anna → L4 LB → WS-Server-12
steps.note: The L4 balancer only picked the server when the socket was opened; frames now flow over the same TCP connection.

steps.cap: WS-Server-12 forwards the message over gRPC to Chat Service, synchronously: the socket waits for the answer.
steps.say: W S Server twelve forwards the message over G R P C to Chat Service, synchronously: the socket waits for the answer.
steps.code:
gRPC Chat.Send(
  chat_id: 'c_77', client_msg_id: 'u-9f3c…',
  sender: 'anna', text: 'Hello')

steps.cap: Chat Service runs SET NX on the idempotency key: if the key exists, this is a retry and it returns the same seq_id as before. If it is new, INCR chat_seq gives the next number, 1042: an atomic single-threaded counter, so two messages in one chat never share a number.
steps.say: Chat Service runs set N X on the idempotency key: if the key exists, this is a retry and it returns the same sequence I D as before. If it is new, increment chat seq gives the next number, one thousand forty-two: an atomic single-threaded counter, so two messages in one chat never share a number.
steps.title: Chat Service → Redis: dedupe, then sequence
steps.code:
SET idem:c_77:u-9f3c… 1042 NX EX 86400
→ OK     new message
→ (nil)  retry: return the stored seq_id

INCR chat_seq:c_77 → 1042

steps.cap: It writes the message to Kafka with partition key chat_id and acks=all: it waits until at least two brokers have it on disk. Log first, database later.
steps.say: It writes the message to Kafka with partition key chat I D and acks equals all: it waits until at least two brokers have it on disk. Log first, database later.
steps.code:
produce messages
  key:   'c_77'      -- same partition
  value: { seq_id: 1042, client_msg_id,
           sender, text }
  acks:  all → partition 7, offset 88213
steps.note: No outbox here: Kafka is the write-ahead log. The database is filled from it afterwards.

steps.cap: Only then does Chat Service answer the WS server, and the WS server answers the phone: one checkmark, SENT. From here on Anna waits for nothing.
steps.say: Only then does Chat Service answer the W S server, and the W S server answers the phone: one checkmark, sent. From here on Anna waits for nothing.
steps.title: SENT: one checkmark

steps.cap: Delivery Worker pulls the message from Kafka at its own pace and asks Redis for Boris's sessions: his phone is on WS-Server-45, his laptop on WS-Server-7.
steps.say: Delivery Worker pulls the message from Kafka at its own pace and asks Redis for Boris's sessions: his phone is on W S Server forty-five, his laptop on W S Server seven.
steps.title: Delivery Worker finds Boris
steps.code:
consumer group 'deliver'
  ← partition 7, offset 88213
HGETALL user_sessions:boris
→ { phone:  'WS-Server-45',
    laptop: 'WS-Server-7' }

steps.cap: It publishes the message on the Redis Pub/Sub channels ws:WS-Server-45 and ws:WS-Server-7; each server is subscribed to its own channel and writes the frame into the right socket.
steps.say: It publishes the message on the Redis pub sub channels for W S Server forty-five and W S Server seven; each server is subscribed to its own channel and writes the frame into the right socket.
steps.title: Redis Pub/Sub → WS-Server-45 → Boris

steps.cap: In parallel and independently, Persist Worker reads the same message from Kafka in another consumer group and writes it to Cassandra, partitioned by chat and time bucket, in batches, as an idempotent upsert.
steps.title: Persist Worker, in parallel
steps.code:
consumer group 'persist' ← offset 88213
INSERT INTO messages
  (chat_id, bucket, seq_id, sender, text)
VALUES ('c_77', '2026-10', 1042,
        'anna', 'Hello');
-- batch of 500, same key = same row

steps.cap: When Boris's phone receives the message, it returns an ACK with the seq_id over its socket; WS-Server-45 publishes a DELIVERED event to Kafka through the same path.
steps.say: When Boris's phone receives the message, it returns an ack with the sequence I D over its socket; W S Server forty-five publishes a delivered event to Kafka through the same path.
steps.title: ACK → DELIVERED event

steps.cap: The same delivery path carries the event to Anna's phone: the second checkmark.
steps.title: Second checkmark

steps.cap: Boris is in airplane mode and the TTL on his sessions has expired. Delivery Worker asks Redis and gets an empty hash: nowhere to deliver.
steps.say: Boris is in airplane mode and the T T L on his sessions has expired. Delivery Worker asks Redis and gets an empty hash: nowhere to deliver.
steps.title: No live sessions
steps.code:
HGETALL user_sessions:boris
→ {}    -- no heartbeat for 60 s, key expired

steps.cap: So it publishes to the Kafka topic push and commits its offset right away, after the attempt, not after an ACK from the phone. Otherwise one offline user would block the partition for everyone else in it.
steps.say: So it publishes to the Kafka topic push and commits its offset right away, after the attempt, not after an ack from the phone. Otherwise one offline user would block the partition for everyone else in it.
steps.title: Delivery Worker → topic push → Push Worker
steps.code:
produce push
  { user: 'boris', chat_id: 'c_77',
    seq_id: 1042, preview: 'Anna' }
commit offset 88213
-- the message is safe in Kafka + Cassandra
steps.note: The message is not lost: it waits in the log and in the history until Boris comes back.

steps.cap: Push Worker reads it and sends a notification through FCM or APNs: only 'New message from Anna', never the text. Push is best effort, not a transport channel.
steps.say: Push Worker reads it and sends a notification through F C M or A P N s: only New message from Anna, never the text. Push is best effort, not a transport channel.
steps.title: Push Worker → FCM / APNs → Boris
steps.code:
POST https://fcm.googleapis.com/v1/
     projects/…/messages:send
{ token: 'd8e…',
  notification:
    { title: 'Anna', body: 'New message' } }

steps.cap: If 20 messages arrive while he is offline, Push Worker folds them into one notification. The messages themselves stay in Kafka and Cassandra, waiting for him.
steps.say: If twenty messages arrive while he is offline, Push Worker folds them into one notification. The messages themselves stay in Kafka and Cassandra, waiting for him.
steps.title: Coalescing
steps.code:
20 push events for boris within 30 s
→ 1 notification: 'Anna: 20 new messages'

scenes.title: Boris lands: reconnect and catch up

steps.cap: Boris lands and his phone connects to any WS server, say WS-Server-3. No sticky sessions: the registry in Redis says where everyone is, so any server will do. The server registers the session with HSET.
steps.say: Boris lands and his phone connects to any W S server, say W S Server three. No sticky sessions: the registry in Redis says where everyone is, so any server will do. The server registers the session with H set.
steps.title: Boris → L4 LB → WS-Server-3 → Redis
steps.code:
WSS /ws → WS-Server-3
HSET user_sessions:boris phone WS-Server-3
EXPIRE user_sessions:boris 60
-- refreshed by every heartbeat

steps.cap: The phone remembers last_seen_seq = 1039 for the chat with Anna and asks over REST: GET /chats/c_77/messages?since=1039. API Gateway forwards it over gRPC to Chat Service, which reads messages 1040, 1041 and 1042 from Cassandra.
steps.say: The phone remembers last seen sequence one thousand thirty-nine for the chat with Anna and asks over rest: get the messages since one thousand thirty-nine. A P I Gateway forwards it over G R P C to Chat Service, which reads messages one thousand forty, forty-one and forty-two from Cassandra.
steps.title: GET /messages?since=1039
steps.code:
GET /chats/c_77/messages?since=1039
→ gRPC Chat.History(
    chat_id: 'c_77', since: 1039)
SELECT * FROM messages
 WHERE chat_id = 'c_77'
   AND bucket = '2026-10'
   AND seq_id > 1039 ORDER BY seq_id;

steps.cap: The three messages come back; the phone merges them and moves last_seen_seq to 1042.
steps.say: The three messages come back; the phone merges them and moves last seen sequence to one thousand forty-two.
steps.title: Chat Service → Boris

steps.cap: Later, if a message with seq_id 1045 arrives over the WebSocket while the phone has only seen up to 1043, the phone itself notices the gap, 1044 is missing, and fetches it. Duplicates from at-least-once delivery are recognised by client_msg_id.
steps.say: Later, if a message with sequence one thousand forty-five arrives over the websocket while the phone has only seen up to one thousand forty-three, the phone itself notices the gap, forty-four is missing, and fetches it. Duplicates from at-least-once delivery are recognised by client message I D.
steps.title: Gap detection on the client
steps.code:
received seq_id 1045, last_seen 1043
→ gap: 1044
GET /chats/c_77/messages?since=1043
seen client_msg_id? → drop duplicate

steps.cap: In Slack with 200 channels the phone does not ask each one: GET /sync?since=cursor returns the last seq_id per channel. And on reconnect clients use backoff with jitter, so 50 000 of them do not come back in the same millisecond after a server restart.
steps.say: In Slack with two hundred channels the phone does not ask each one: a single sync request returns the last sequence per channel. And on reconnect clients use backoff with jitter, so fifty thousand of them do not come back in the same millisecond after a server restart.
steps.title: Resync cursor, reconnect with jitter
steps.note: A thundering herd of reconnects is a self-inflicted outage; jitter spreads it over seconds.

recap.title: What to say in the interview
recap.closing:
The log is the truth.
The socket is just a wire.

items.text: Send over the open WebSocket, then gRPC to Chat Service
items.cap: To sum up. A message goes over the already open WebSocket and then over gRPC to Chat Service.
items.say: To sum up. A message goes over the already open websocket and then over G R P C to Chat Service.

items.text: SET NX for idempotency, INCR for a monotonic seq_id per chat
items.cap: SET NX on the client's message id makes retries safe, and INCR gives a monotonic sequence number per chat.
items.say: Set N X on the client's message I D makes retries safe, and increment gives a monotonic sequence number per chat.

items.text: Kafka acks=all before SENT: log first, database later
items.cap: Kafka with acks=all comes before the SENT checkmark: log first, database later.
items.say: Kafka with acks equals all comes before the sent checkmark: log first, database later.

items.text: Independent consumer groups: deliver, persist, push, index
items.cap: Delivery, persistence, push and search are independent consumer groups, so a slow database never delays delivery.

items.text: Session registry in Redis, resync by seq_id, backoff with jitter
items.cap: And a session registry in Redis, resync by sequence number and backoff with jitter handle offline users and reconnects. The log is the truth; the socket is just a wire.
